bull_bear.body:
- **No equity raise needed for ~2–2.5 years.** Leverage **3.15x** today. *"once it approaches the 4 to 4.5 levels, that's when we'll need to look at fresh capital, but till then we don't need. And basic internal calculations that we've done, that would mean that we have enough capital for the next 2 to two and a half years of growth."* Quantified: *"if we take a leverage of 4 to 4.5 times before we raise money, it means that we can grow our book to almost INR14,000 crores. We are today sitting at INR7,384 crores. So, this gives us a window of slightly more than 2 years, 2.5 years before we'll need money."*
- **Low ROE is an explicit, temporary consequence of the IPO**, not an earnings-power statement: *"The reason you are seeing low ROEs is because we have recently raised money through IPO and therefore our leverage is very small. And this leverage will gradually grow."*
- **Profits are being deliberately reserved into overlays in a good year** — a counter-cyclical allocation choice: *"we will continue to absorb some of the profits into these overlays, because this is a good year and we believe that in good years we should create that overlay... last quarter was robust quarter on profits and we have taken out INR6 crores out of that to put into the overlay."* Target 0.5% of book.
- **DA capped by policy at 5–7% of AUM**, currently 5% — used for liquidity and P&L, not as a growth crutch: *"we are not very aggressively posturing on DA... We don't want to do more DAs."*
- **Co-lending explicitly rejected on unit economics** — see §12.
- No dividend, buyback or M&A discussed.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
1. **Monsoon.** Management quantified rather than dismissed it: *"if you go to the IMD site, it states that the expectation they have, and I'm quoting from that site, is about 92% of the long-term average of rainfall plus-minus 5%. So, irrespective of what we may feel, the monsoons are below normal but not substantially below that number."* Geographic mitigant: *"most of the effect of lower rainfall or deficit rainfall will be seen in only central India and southern peninsula"*, while *"our large states like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, et cetera, which account for significant share of the portfolio... are the states which are not expected to be affected by the issues of monsoon this year."* **Watch: this is a forecast-based comfort, testable at Q2.**
2. **West Asia war** — flagged at the start of the year as an imponderable, now *"the fear of impact of West Asia war has got moderated."* Q1 showed *"no signs of any sort of impact of the market imponderables."*
3. **Mortgage deep-bucket collections are an admitted capability gap** (§5) — PAR 90 gap to hypothecation ~2.5%, and the collections infrastructure is still being built.
4. **Credit cost sits at the very top of the guided band (4.01% vs 3.5–4.0%)** and is flattered by nothing — but it *includes* a ~INR6cr overlay creation, so the underlying is lower while the reported is at the ceiling. Any cycle turn removes the overlay cushion (total overlay only INR11cr).
5. **Opex above the guided band (8.9% vs 8.25–8.75%)** with the branch and manpower build still ahead in Q2–Q3 — the ratio depends on the AUM denominator growing faster than the cost base.
6. **PAR X did not improve** — 6.9% → 7.01% — even as GNPA and credit cost did. Explained as a denominator effect, but it is the one metric that moved the wrong way.
7. **Slippage is not disclosed.** *"we haven't reported slippage number. I do not have that number readily available and we can share that eventually."* A gap for anyone modelling the credit cycle independently.
8. **Guidance credibility risk in both directions** — every metric is running better than guidance, guidance was left unchanged, and a refinement was promised for Q2. Under-promising is benign; a *failure* to refine upward at Q2 would read as caution the numbers don't yet show.
9. **Concentration in the hypothecation product** — 78% of book in a 24-month unsecured-ish working-capital product with 5.5–6% terminal losses.
10. **Analyst pushback on peer comparison of credit cost** (opening question) — management's defence is that the products are not comparable: *"in our model, each product category has a different credit cost model and therefore it's incorrect to compare one segment against the other."*
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body:
Confident, unusually specific, and notably willing to give numbers that do not flatter.

- **Volunteers its own weaknesses.** The mortgage deep-bucket collection gap, the missing slippage disclosure, PAR X ticking up, and opex being outside the band were all conceded plainly rather than deflected.
- **Self-corrects in the document.** The transcript carries a printed errata on capital adequacy (41.3% → 42.4%) — a sign of a controlled disclosure process.
- **Deliberately conservative on guidance while acknowledging the upside**, which is the tone signature of this call. On NIM: *"clearly I think even I would have had the same question that if everything seems to be working in one direction, why is the guidance different? But I think there's an upside there."* And: *"We have moved very close to that band much quicker than expected... I think that we are going to wait for one more quarter."*
- **Frames the caution as macro-uncertainty resolution, not sandbagging:** *"in quarter 2, the fuzziness that was there in quarter 1, the war was there, then everyone was saying that huge amount of inflation will happen, then everyone thought that there's going to be a drought across the country. Those are becoming clearer."*
- **Cites external sources rather than asserting** — quoted the IMD site directly for the monsoon view, including the unflattering *"the monsoons are below normal."*
- **Admits missing data instead of guessing.** On whether gold-loan borrowers collect better: *"we don't have that data upfront... my guess would be that there might not be that much of a correlation... But we don't have the data for that. Maybe later on we can probably share some data on that."*
- **Deep operating fluency** — LTVs, pre-closure rates, attachment rates, branch-vintage AUM distribution, bucket-level collection efficiency all answered without deferral, mostly by Sovan Satyaprakash and Gaurav Seth.
- Minor negative: two management statements on the same call give different AUM (INR7,324cr vs INR7,384cr) and different manpower-growth figures (10% vs 13–15%), neither reconciled.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
1. **The reject pile is a distribution asset.** Declining ~55,000 customers a quarter — more than they approve — is normally pure sunk cost. Management reframed it as the sourcing funnel for a future gold-loan book: *"These customers in the end go and seek a gold loan, a substantial part, 20% plus do that. So, we have the ability to source and we are not fully leveraging that ability to source customers."* A tightened credit filter (55% → 45% approval) *increases* the size of this asset.
2. **Terminal loss is identical across a secured and a quasi-secured product** — *"the terminal losses that we observe across both the products, be it a Micro LAP product or a hypothecation product, remain very much in the same range of about 5.5% to about 6%."* This undercuts the usual assumption that the mortgage shift is a credit-quality trade; the gain is in *timing and yearly translation*, not ultimate loss.
3. **Co-lending is rejected on arithmetic, not principle** — a rare, concrete explanation of why small-ticket lenders can't play the co-lending game: *"because our ticket size is very small, so therefore doing all the hard work of originating it and then finding that I can only keep 20% of the INR1 lakhs loan does not work in my favor because it doesn't defray my cost... Despite the fact that the loan is as small as INR1-1.5 lakhs, our processing fee is still 2.5%. You can think about that, it's only INR2,500. Many of the mortgage players would take more than that only for the legal technical fees."*
4. **Government credit guarantees are being declined as uneconomic** — the opposite of the usual NBFC posture: *"CGMFU we have only done 4.5% of our book on CGMFU because we don't see a huge benefit coming because our credit costs are low and well-managed."* A quiet confidence signal.
5. **The digital-lending threat is dismissed with a data argument, not bravado.** Only 10–20% of borrower transactions pass through UPI (*"which we can see through the account aggregator data"*), and QR volume is *"between about 15% to 20% at max"* of business volume — *"we do feel that is not enough of data point to really offer a business loan."* The cash economy of tier-2/3 India is the moat, and it is measurable.
6. **They have the fintech capability and chose not to scale it.** 7–8% of fresh sourcing is digital; asked whether they deploy QR/payment infrastructure: *"No, we are not in that line of sourcing... our originating costs are lower"* than UPI-based sourcing. A deliberate rejection of the fashionable channel.
7. **Interest-reversal reduction is a hidden NIM tailwind that no one models**, because the driver — slippages — isn't disclosed. Management named it as the #2 NIM driver while simultaneously confirming the number isn't published.
8. **Mortgage delinquency is a two-state problem, not a product problem** — *"many of those delinquency is concentrated in couple of states rather than a widespread delinquency."* That reframes a product-quality worry into an execution-scope worry.
9. **Branch splits are profitable from day one** — *"they are positive or profitable from day one itself"* — meaning ~60-70% of the network sitting at INR7-8cr average AUM is a self-funding growth pipeline that doesn't show up as capex.
10. **Cross-sell income is structurally protected from IRDA commission caps** because Aye is a corporate agent with its own licence, not a commission recipient — an answer given to a question that assumed the opposite risk.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Networth of Rs. 2,603 Crore and book value per share of Rs. 106 as of 30th June 2026; networth progression is 1,236 (Mar-24), 1,658 (Mar-25), 2,533 (Mar-26) and 2,603 (Jun-26).
- Capital adequacy ratio of 42.4% at Jun-26 (32.8% Mar-24, 34.9% Mar-25, 42.2% Mar-26), with leverage of 3.15x in Q1FY27 (3.88x in Q1FY26) and closing D/E of 2.13x — a heavily over-capitalised balance sheet relative to the guided growth.
- Rs 710 crores of equity was infused in Feb-26; the deck marks Q1FY26 and Q4FY26 RoE figures with an asterisk noting this infusion, and RoE stands at 11.68% for Q1FY27 versus 7.40% in Q1FY26 and 15.98% in Q4FY26.
- Funding is diversified across Banks (32.0%), Development Financial Institutions (19.1%) and Financial Institutions (49.0%, including 12.2% of retail borrowings), with debt raised of Rs 1,136.7 crores in Q1FY27; the deck states there is no ALM mismatch in cashflow in any tenor bucket and that the company is well positioned to increase the average tenor of assets.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

business.body:
No subsidiaries were discussed. The business splits by **product**:

**Hypothecation loans (the core engine, ~78% of book by implication of the 22% mortgage share)**
- Working-capital loan to micro-enterprises; *"typically with a tenor of about 24 months and INR1.5 lakhs average ticket size."*
- Portfolio ROI **27.5% to ~28%**. LTV *"somewhere around 60 odd percentage on the inventory levels."*
- Pre-closure rate: *"typically we see annualized pre-closure rates of roughly around 3 to 3.5 odd percentage"* — i.e. very sticky.
- *"Hypothecation loan is the driving engine for the business model and hypothecation loan productivity has significantly improved. The productivity levels that we saw in quarter 1 are very much in line with productivity levels of quarter 2 and quarter 3 of last financial year."*
- Demand fit: *"They want a typical working capital loan of INR1 to INR2 lakhs. So, it addresses a real market need."*

**Mortgage / Micro-LAP (22% of portfolio)**
- Portfolio ROI **~23.5%**; LTV *"about 35% to 40%."*
- Newer: *"Mortgage for us is a new investment that we have done over the last three years."*
- **The identified weak spot is deep-bucket collections, not origination:** *"while we have built capacity with respect to disbursements and distribution network and we are seeing very good collection levels in the non-OD category. We are yet to build a strong capacity with respect to further recoveries and in the deeper buckets."* Remediation is underway: *"over the last 1 quarter, 2 quarters, our endeavor has been to increase the collection infrastructure in mortgage so that our ability to collect in the delinquent buckets improves."*
- Delinquency is geographically concentrated, which management reads as tractable: *"many of those delinquency is concentrated in couple of states rather than a widespread delinquency that we see across all states where we do mortgage. So, it is more to tackle in those two odd states."*
- Higher pre-closure than hypothecation *"because of the nature of the business and BT outs and BT ins that happen over the industry"* — blended pre-closure 5–5.5%, offset by *"we are getting foreclosure charges from the BT out cases."*

**Terminal loss economics are the same across both products** — an important, non-obvious statement: *"the terminal losses that we observe across both the products, be it a Micro LAP product or a hypothecation product, remain very much in the same range of about 5.5% to about 6%. But when you look at from a yearly credit loss or cost standpoint, this usually translates between 3.5% or so."*

**Cross-sell / insurance distribution** — three products, attachment rates *"the lowest product would be the attachment rate of roughly around 20% or so, while the highest product could be in the range of about 90%."* INR9cr income this quarter.

**Government-guarantee cover is deliberately thin:** *"In terms of the ECLGS, we have a ECLGS scheme ongoing, where the book is around 4.5%"* — and the reason it is not larger: *"the reason that you'll find that CGMFU we have only done 4.5% of our book on CGMFU because we don't see a huge benefit coming because our credit costs are low and well-managed."*
business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body:
Evidenced on this call with specific numbers, not asserted:

- **Cost position at one-third the peer ticket size.** *"my ticket size on an average is INR1.5 lakhs, their ticket size on an average is about INR4.5 lakhs, it's about 3 times the ticket. They have a cost operating expense of about 4% to 5%. With the one-third the product scale, I am able to manage it in that 9% range."* And the mechanism: *"why are we able to do it in 9% instead of 15% if I just take proportionate operating expense is primarily through use of data, high productivity of the loan officer, and many other parameters which bring in efficiency into the process."*
- **Recovery capability far above the MFI comparator — the strongest single moat datapoint on the call.** *"MFI industry after PAR 90, their collection efficiency beyond PAR 90 is anyway between 5% to 8%, 9%. Our collection efficiency after PAR 90 is close to 29% to 30%. So, there's a big collection that we do."* The consequence: *"if your collection from PAR 90 is hardly 5% to 8%, the only way for dramatic reduction in PAR 90 is through write-off. It can't be collection. We have not gone for aggressive write-offs because we know that whatever is sitting in our PAR 90, it may be 4% or 5%, we will collect one-third of that at least."*
- **Underwriting on cluster-based alternate data, built for a cash economy** — the barrier that keeps digital lenders out. *"our models are built on the fact that there'll be a lot of cash-based transaction, therefore underwriting is based on a cluster-based alternate data, not looking at the balance or the bank statement or UPI-based transaction."*
- **Hiring is not a constraint because they do not compete for scarce NBFC talent.** *"we don't rely only on the NBFC industry experienced people for hiring. We can hire fresh staff also, we have trainees that we hire, we can even hire from the MFI market, because we have a very strong training program."*
- **Distribution breadth:** 571 branches, 18 states + 3 UTs — *"that is one unique strength that we carry that we can generate 44,000 loans in a single quarter despite tightening of credit."* Demand *"is spread across the entire country, so it's not coming from one particular part of the country."*
- **Own IRDA corporate-agency licence rather than a commission arrangement** — insulates cross-sell income from any commission cap: *"we have a corporate agency. So, it is not done through a commission being paid et cetera. We are a corporate agent. We have taken a formal corporate agency license from IRDA and we have people in our team who have passed that examination."*
business.title: 6a. Moat & competitive position

business.body:
> Only challenges Aye **specifically discussed on this call**. Names resolved against `output/concall/companies.csv` + `products.csv` first; unresolved names are left blank rather than sourced externally. ✅=covered in our universe, ⭐=sector knowledge.

| Challenge (their words) | Beneficiary stock(s) — NSE · BSE · Sector | Loser | Why / conviction |
|---|---|---|---|
| *"the monsoons are below normal but not substantially below that number... most of the effect of lower rainfall or deficit rainfall will be seen in only central India and southern peninsula"* | Lenders concentrated in the **north/east** rain-fed belt Aye names as unaffected (Bihar, UP, Rajasthan) — AYE itself ✅; SATIN · 539404 · Microfinance-led rural NBFC ✅ (north-India-weighted JLG book) | Rural lenders weighted to **central India / southern peninsula**; no name in our files resolves cleanly to that footprint → **unmapped** | Med. Aye's own framing is geographic, and the read-through is a footprint call, not a product call. Conviction capped because the monsoon outcome is an IMD *forecast* at call date |
| *"the terminal losses... remain very much in the same range of about 5.5% to about 6%"* — i.e. micro-MSME credit is structurally loss-heavy, and *"our opex... 9% as compared to 4%-5% say for microfinance"* | Scale MFI/SFB models whose **group-lending origination avoids income underwriting cost**: UJJIVANSFB · 542904 · SFB ✅; UTKARSHBNK · 543942 · SFB ✅; SATIN · 539404 ✅ | Sub-scale micro-MSME lenders that must carry underwriting + monitoring cost without Aye's density or data — **unmapped** (no comparable listed micro-enterprise hypothecation pure-play in our files) | Med. Management drew this comparison itself and explained the cost gap mechanically; it is a genuine cost-structure divide, not commentary |
| *"we also decline close to 55,000 customers. These customers in the end go and seek a gold loan, a substantial part, 20% plus do that"* + *"10% to 12% of the people have gold loans"* | **Gold-loan NBFCs** — the direct recipients of Aye's rejects and of 10–12% of its borrower base. No gold-loan pure-play resolves in `companies.csv` (MUTHOOTFIN / MANAPPURAM / CGCL all absent) → **unmapped**, per the no-external-lookup rule ⭐ | Aye today (foregone volume), until its own gold product launches | High on the mechanism (management quantified both the reject flow and the 20%+ conversion), but **beneficiary deliberately left unmapped** — no listed gold-loan name exists in our own files |
| *"there is certainly an overlap, but it's not a very large overlap"* with merchant/QR lenders; *"the usage of QR code for trading or payments from their overall volume of business is still minimal"* — digital lenders can't underwrite the cash economy | AYE ✅ and other **branch-led, alternate-data underwriters** — the cash-transaction share is the barrier that protects them | PAYTM · 543396 · Fintech / Digital Payments & Financial-Services Distribution ✅ (named on the call as the merchant-loan comparator); MOBIKWIK · 544305 · Consumer fintech — payments + digital lending ✅ ⭐ | Med. Management named Paytm explicitly and sized the overlap with account-aggregator data (10–20% of transactions via UPI), but framed loans from such players as small (INR30,000–50,000) and non-competitive rather than a share threat |
| *"because our ticket size is very small... I can only keep 20% of the INR1 lakhs loan does not work in my favor because it doesn't defray my cost"* — co-lending economics fail below a ticket threshold | **Larger-ticket lenders** for whom co-lending economics do work: SAMMAANCAP · 535789 · Housing finance NBFC ✅; NORTHARC · 544260 · Diversified NBFC / credit platform ✅ (co-lending & securitization platform); MANBA · 544262 · Vehicle-finance NBFC ✅ | Banks/NBFCs seeking PSL assets via co-lending from small-ticket originators — Aye will not supply them | Med. A clean, quantified structural boundary; the beneficiary set follows directly from ticket size |
| *"we did not undertake any DA, the direct assignment deal during the quarter... Last quarter, DA had contributed to around INR20 crores"* + policy cap of 5–7% of AUM | **PSL-asset buyers lose a supplier**; securitization/DA platforms that intermediate elsewhere: NORTHARC · 544260 ✅ (credit-solutions/securitization platform) | Banks needing PSL-eligible micro-enterprise pools — Aye is post-IPO capital-rich and structurally reducing DA supply | Low–Med. The Q1 gap is capital-driven and reversible; the 5–7% cap is the durable part |
| *"CGMFU we have only done 4.5% of our book on CGMFU because we don't see a huge benefit coming"* — guarantee schemes under-consumed by strong-credit lenders | — (no listed beneficiary; the counterparty is a government guarantee fund, not a listed entity) | Weaker-credit micro-lenders that must pay for guarantee cover Aye can skip — **unmapped** | Low. Directionally informative about relative credit confidence; no listed read-through |

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers (listed names)

business.body:
- Targets the "Unorganised Micro MSME" segment — customers with no financial documents, turnover of Rs 30 lakhs to Rs 1 crore p.a. and income of Rs 5-15 lakhs p.a. — a niche the deck places between MFIs/marginal borrowers below and banks/organised MSME lenders above.
- Moat framed as a proprietary underwriting methodology developed for 70+ unique business clusters (vertical clusters such as power loom, leather goods, brass work and horizontal ones such as grocery, eatery, salon), with high entry barriers from technology adoption, underwriting and collections capability.
- 100% in-house origination model with a branch-led distribution network of 571 branches across 18 states and 3 UTs serving ~6.7 lakh active customers; average ticket size of Rs 1.7 lakhs is cited as evidence of financial-inclusion reach and portfolio granularity.
- Customer profile filters stated: permanent business setup for at least 2 years, predominantly Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, average customer turnover of INR 2.00-10.00 million, and 95%+ of customers owning their residence and/or place of business.
- Backed by Elevation Capital, Temasek Trust Asset Management, Google Capital, A91 Investments, British International Investment, Lightrock and Alpha Wave; the FY2026 milestone on the journey slide is the Initial Public Offering.
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Asset quality] Management states GNPA at 4.49%, improving 28 bps sequentially and marking the sixth consecutive quarter of improvement, with PAR X at 7.01%, PAR 30 stable at 6.07%, credit cost moderating to 4.01% (down 29 bps QoQ), Non-OD collection efficiency at 99.2% and Bucket 1 collections at 54.5%.
- [Provisioning] As of 30th June 2026 gross loans outstanding were Rs 6,865 crores across Stage 1 (6,475), Stage 2 (83) and Stage 3 (308), with ECL provision of Rs 275 crores (0.65% / 47.11% / 63.05% by stage, 4.01% total, excluding management overlay); PCR as of 30th June 2026 is 63.80%.
- [Vintage of book] 92% of the portfolio has been originated post the volatile period of market over-lending (post Jun-24), and the average annualized foreclosure rate for Q1FY27 was 5.65%.
- [Shareholding] More-than-5% holders as of 30th June 2026: Elevation Capital 12.6%, LGT Capital Invest 10.1%, Alpha Wave India 7.8%, CapitalG LP (erstwhile Google Capital) 7.7%, British International Investment 7.4%, A91 Emerging Fund 7.2% and Imp2 Assets (Temasek Trust Asset Management) 5.5%.
- [Outlook] Management expects business momentum to further improve in Q2FY27, supported by improving customer demand, stable collections and a more favourable operating environment.
business.title: Notable from the deck

latest_quarter.body:
**NIM rose against the mix headwind — the central margin story.** Three drivers named explicitly by Sanjay Sharma:
1. **Mix (negative):** *"the movement of mix towards the mortgage piece of the portfolio. Because mortgage is at a lower rate, it tends to bring the NIM down."*
2. **Interest reversals (positive, and quantified only qualitatively):** *"the amount of reversals that you make, because when things go into NPA, you have to reverse out the interest of the previous months as well. That reversal, because the slippages into NPA is reducing, we have an upside on that. We haven't mentioned the slippages number, but that is one of the things that the reducing slippages causing a upside on the NIM."*
3. **Borrowing cost (positive):** *"our borrowing rates, because they have been dropping and plus the new rating that has come in will see that play out."*

Net: *"as we saw in first quarter, that reduction is more than made up by the reduction in the finance cost even as the percentage of borrowing cost. So, this actually compensates for that and in fact that's the reason in quarter 1 we've seen an increase in our NIM. This trend is expected to continue through the year."*

**Cost of funds is falling on three legs:** weighted cost 10.87% → **10.78%**; incremental at **~10.20%** (*"nearly 60 bps lower"*); plus an unbooked **10–15bps** from the rating upgrade (the upgrade's full-year effect was separately framed as **20–25bps on incremental borrowings**).

**Opex is converging on the band from above, with an explicit denominator argument.** 9.5% (Q4 last year) → **8.9%** now, target 8.25–8.75%. *"the new branch investment is not a large investment with respect to opex. Considering the fact that we are already 11,000 manpower company and we're adding about 40 odd branches is not going to be a significant number of people to be added."* CFO: *"last year we ended Q4 at 9.5%, today we are already at a 8.9% and therefore we are actually walking the path of getting to the 8.25%-8.75% range."*

**Why opex is structurally ~2x an MFI:** *"there is a credit underwriting that is done in our process, which is absent in the MFI process. That itself adds to the cost. Second is that because it's a business loan, it also needs monitoring... Originating in the MFI world is done through a group process, therefore it makes it easy to acquire customers, especially since there is no income underwriting."*

**Credit cost mechanics:** 4.01%, down 29bps QoQ, driven by *"tighter underwriting standards, stronger collection efforts, a growth of mortgage loans within the portfolio, and improving repayment behavior among our customers as business cash flows continue to strengthen."* Management's structural claim: *"these developments reinforce our belief that the improvements in portfolio quality that we are seeing are structural and sustainable."*

**Longer-term credit-cost path is mix-driven:** *"with mortgage increasing eventually, and not in this financial year but eventually increasing to about 30%, we can safely assume about a 50 bps lower levels on the credit cost. So, the range that we should be targeting once mortgage hits about 30% would be in the range of about 3% to maybe a 3.25% or 3.5% at max."*

**The PAR X → credit cost link, stated as a rule:** *"if our PAR X remains at 7%, we will ultimately hit a credit cost of 3.5% to 4%. In fact, if it remains at 7%, we're likely that we'll hit a credit cost of 3.5%... yes, 7% is good enough."* Sustainable target: *"a good level to target is 6% to 6.5 odd percentage."*
latest_quarter.title: Margins & cost dynamics

latest_quarter.body:
- **Q1 FY27 (this):** Record Q1 disbursement INR1,219cr (+22% YoY); AUM INR7,324cr (+28% YoY, +4% QoQ). **Sixth consecutive quarter of asset-quality improvement** — GNPA 4.49% (from 4.77%), credit cost 4.01% (−29bps QoQ). PAT INR75cr (+144% YoY) on gross total income INR490cr (+22%) and net total income INR322cr (+38%). **NIM rose 20bps QoQ to 15.9% despite the mortgage mix shift** — 115–165bps above the 14.25–14.75% guided band. India Ratings upgrade IND A → A+ / A1 → A1+, worth 20–25bps on incremental borrowings, **not yet in the run-rate**. Approval rate tightened 55% → 45% yet 44,000+ borrowers added (+38% YoY). Leverage only 3.15x post-IPO; no capital needed for 2–2.5 years. Fee income optically weak on two prior-quarter one-offs (~INR32–33cr: no DA + FX moved to OCI). ~INR6cr overlay created (total INR11cr). **All FY27 guidance reaffirmed, none raised**, with a refinement promised at end-Q2. Watch-items: PAR X ticked up 6.9% → 7.01%; opex 8.9% vs 8.25–8.75% band; mortgage deep-bucket collections still being built.
- _Q2 FY27 → check: (1) **did the promised guidance refinement actually arrive**, and was NIM/credit-cost guidance raised? (2) branch adds — the 40–50 for the year were back-loaded into Q2–Q3, watch slippage; (3) PAR X reverting below 7% as the denominator grows; (4) opex moving into the 8.25–8.75% band; (5) the 10–15bps incremental-borrowing benefit from the rating upgrade showing up in cost of funds; (6) monsoon outcome vs the IMD 92%-of-LTA forecast, especially Bihar/UP/Rajasthan collection efficiency; (7) mortgage PAR 90 improving from ~3% as collection infrastructure lands; (8) any gold-loan launch decision after the market survey; (9) whether slippage is finally disclosed._
latest_quarter.title: QoQ change log (fill each quarter)

outlook.body:
All FY27 guidance **reaffirmed, not raised**, despite Q1 running ahead on nearly every line.

- **AUM growth:** *"We are targeting an AUM growth, as we had said in the guidance, between 25% to 30% for this year."* Q1 delivered +28% YoY / +4% QoQ.
- **Credit cost:** **3.5% to 4.0%** for FY27. *"Our guidance on credit cost was, and at the beginning of the year we had given a guidance of 3.5% to 4%, and this appears well within our grasp now."* Q1 actual 4.01% — i.e. at the **top** of the band. *"Quarter 1 has definitely been encouraging where we are already at the top of that band."* Guidance **includes** creation and utilization of overlays — confirmed twice: *"creation of overlays will not be outside this credit cost number... that would be what our endeavor would be, to stay in the guidance range."*
- **NIM:** guidance **14.25% to 14.75%**, unchanged, vs 15.9% actual. Management conceded an upside: *"See, I think there is an upside that is possible on that number."* And: *"we therefore are guiding that NIM will remain flat, it will not come down."*
- **Opex ratio:** **8.25% to 8.75%** for FY27 vs 8.9% in Q1. *"we did realize that quarter 1, quarter 2 we might be out of those bands and quarter 3, quarter 4 we will be very much in the band giving a result which for the entire year should be in that band."* 3-year path: *"this should gradually tend towards 7% to 7.5% in the next 3 years."*
- **ROA target:** *"at a credit cost of 3.5% to 4%, we will deliver a targeted ROA of 4.5% to 5% post-tax."*
- **Branch additions:** *"we expect to add only around 40 to 50 branches during the year"* — ~10% of the 571 base — *"For this year, that number change will be visible between quarter 2 to quarter 3 when the count would increase."* Strategy is deepening, not new geographies.
- **Manpower:** *"at best between 13% to 15% at best is what the manpower increase is going to happen"*; separately Sanjay: *"We only want to grow our team by about 10% further... This 10% growth in team will deliver the AUM growth of around 25% to 30% for us."* (The two figures are stated differently by two speakers on the same call — carried as stated, not reconciled.)
- **Mortgage mix:** *"we intend to gradually increase the share of mortgage loans in our portfolio this year"* — but *"while we are today already at 22% of our portfolio in mortgages, we expect it to only grow marginally through the year."* Eventual target ~30–35%, explicitly **not** this year.
- **DA:** *"As a strategy, we want to limit the DA to between 5% to 7% and that's the long-term strategy. We don't want to do more DAs."* Currently 5% of AUM.
- **Overlay:** *"eventually we want to create about 0.5% of the book as overlay."*
- **⚠️ GUIDANCE REFINEMENT PROMISED FOR Q2** — the single most checkable commitment from this call. *"hopefully, by the end of quarter 2, we will be able to narrow down our guidance to more refined numbers that we see. But we continue to maintain our guidance as we had given during the year."* Echoed by Sovan: *"by end of H1, I think we can give a more tighter guidance and talk of maybe more narrow ranges."*
- **5-year vision (medium-term, not FY27):** AUM of **INR24,000 crores** within 5 years, *"which translates to roughly 27%, 28% CAGR within 5 years"*; targeted mix over the next 3 years — *"we will like to see 60%-70% hypothecation, 30% Micro LAP, and at best 10% can be some other product."*

outlook.body:
Not applicable in the industrial sense — the lender analogue is disbursement, borrower acquisition and funding access.

- **Disbursement INR1,219 crores, +22% YoY** — a record for a first quarter, against a segment that is seasonally the weakest: *"Historically, as I said, this quarter tends to be seasonally softer with economic activity and credit demand moderating after the financial year-end. Despite this seasonal pattern, we have delivered the strongest-ever first-quarter disbursement performance."*
- **Customer acquisition ran hot despite a materially tighter credit filter.** Approval rate cut from 55% to 45%: *"Earlier we used to allow roughly 55% of the cases logged in used to be approved and disbursed. That 55% has shrunk down to 45% and we have continued to keep that policy tight. Despite that tightening of policy, we have continued to see very good customer acquisition."* 44,000+ added, +38% YoY.
- **Funding access is not a constraint.** *"we don't have any challenge around raising funds in the market for our lending. So, we have a very diversified set of borrowers from whom we borrow, which includes lot of mainline banks, private banks, small finance banks, NBFCs, and DFIs."*
- **Rating upgrade improves the funding pipeline.** India Ratings and Research upgraded the long-term rating **IND A → IND A+ (stable outlook)** and commercial paper **IND A1 → A1+**. *"the upgrade further strengthens our funding profile. It is expected to, on one hand, broaden our lender relationships and enhance funding flexibility, and on the other hand, it is also going to reduce our borrowing cost by approximately 20 to 25 basis points on the incremental borrowings over the course of the year."* The benefit is **not yet in the run-rate**: *"The ratings came in towards the fag end of the borrowing cycle and therefore these have not been yet factored into. We expect with this rating upgrade to get additional benefits of between 10 to 15 bps going forward."*
- **Seasonal shape of the year, as stated:** *"40% split of disbursement in H1, about 60% split in H2"*, with Q1 at 20–22% at max. *"March or quarter 4 and more particularly March is a high productive month and high productive quarter."*
outlook.title: Order book & pipeline

outlook.body:
- **Gold loans — the clearest optionality, and it is sourced from their own reject pile.** *"We are realizing that when we give out loans to 44,000 customers in a quarter, we also decline close to 55,000 customers. These customers in the end go and seek a gold loan, a substantial part, 20% plus do that. So, we have the ability to source and we are not fully leveraging that ability to source customers."* Independently, 10–12% of the existing borrower base already has a gold loan: *"out of the total borrower base, I think somewhere in the range of about 10% to 12% of the people have gold loans... we do feel that as a product line which is a huge opportunity for us in the long run."* Status: *"We are in the process of doing a market survey."* **Not launched, not dated.**
- **Solar loans** floated as an adjacent secured product: *"it could be a solar loan also."* Sized modestly — gold/solar/other together *"would probably be only 10% in the next three years."*
- **Branch splitting is the under-appreciated growth lever** — capacity from the existing estate rather than new geography. *"we also every year see a large number of branches which enter into the INR20 crores plus category... we are actively looking at splitting those branches to tap into the micro-market further."* Last year *"we split roughly around 44 odd branches and the levels at which both these branches or after splitting the branches are, they are positive or profitable from day one itself."* Runway: *"many of those 60%-70% of the branches which are with average AUM of roughly around INR7-8 crores, these branches can also attain the scale of 20 plus crores. So, from the existing branch infrastructure, there is a long runway that is available."*
- **Digital sourcing exists but is deliberately sub-scale:** *"we have a team that almost generates close to 7% to 8% of our fresh sourcing comes from that segment. So, we have the fintech capability to do exactly the same. However, we don't see as much of traction on that to make it a substantial channel."*
- **AI/ML already deployed, not aspirational:** *"even in the AI area, we have already had machine learning models and AI-related models deployed over the last few years."*
- **Market headroom is the core growth argument:** *"We have not even penetrated, I would say, 2% or 3% of that market. So, I think when you have a complete white space, there is going to be extended periods of growth."*
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

deepdive.thesis: Aye Finance delivered its strongest-ever first quarter — record Q1 disbursement of INR1,219cr (+22% YoY), AUM INR7,324cr (+28% YoY) — while asset quality improved for a **sixth consecutive quarter** (GNPA 4.49%, credit cost 4.01%) and PAT more than doubled to INR75cr (+144% YoY). The surprise is margin direction: despite a deliberate mix shift toward lower-yield mortgages, NIM **rose** 20bps sequentially to 15.9% because falling borrowing cost more than offset the yield drag, leaving reported NIM ~115–165bps **above** the company's own 14.25–14.75% FY27 guidance band. Post-IPO leverage is only 3.15x against a 41–42% capital adequacy, so the constraint is not capital — it is proving that the credit-cost normalization is structural rather than cyclical.
